newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore should sell SingTel stake - Lee.
newsitem.headline: Singapore should sell SingTel stake - Lee.

text.p: The Singapore government should sell all its remaining shares in telephone monopoly Singapore Telecommunications Ltd (SingTel), the city-state's patriarch Lee Kuan Yew was quoted as saying on Tuesday.

The Business Times newspaper quoted Lee, who was Singapore's prime minister for 31 years until 1990 and now as Senior Minister retains a strong voice in government policy, as saying Singapore had successfully run a mixed economy of private and public enterprises in the past.
But the country must deregulate its system quickly or be "wiped out in five to seven years", the newspaper quoted Lee as saying in an interview.

"Our Telecoms was highly successful as a statutory board. But if we don't get on quickly with deregulation, as has taken place in America and is now spreading throughout Europe and Japan, we would be wiped out in five to seven years," he said.
"How well we succeed depends on how quickly we change the mindset of management. They've got up to the year 2000, this cosy little protected domestic market," Lee said.
"But the government still owns the majority (of) shares. We've got to unload it completely and have it run on 'for profit only' basis, that is, with competitiveness as the only consideration."
One of Lee's sons, Lee Hsien Yang, is president and chief executive officer of SingTel.
Although some of SingTel's more than 15 billion shares have recently been sold to the public, the government still holds about 80 percent of the group.
State investment company Temasek, through which the government's shares are held, announced in August this year a programme to sell 300-450 million shares over three years by private placement.
Bits and pieces of SingTel's market in Singapore have been opened up to competition already, and the government aims to fully deregulate its domestic basic telecommunications market by the year 2000.
Shares in several other government-controlled companies have also been listed in recent years.
But some large enterprises, like Singapore Power and those in the broadcast sector, remain wholly in government hands.
